opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one we think about a lot. Benchmarks are incredibly useful early on. They give you a shared target and a way to measure progress. But once a benchmark becomes the thing everyone optimizes for, it stops telling you what you actually want to know. That's Goodhart's law playing out in real time.

So a few things I'd suggest. First, treat any public benchmark as a sanity check, not a goal. If your model jumps ten points on some leaderboard but users don't feel a difference, that should worry you more than it excites you. The real signal is whether the model is more useful, more reliable, and more capable on things people care about.

Second, invest in held-out and internal evals that nobody is training against, ideally ones that refresh over time. Contamination is a real problem. A lot of benchmark data ends up on the internet and in pretraining corpora, so you need fresh problems to know whether the model is reasoning or just remembering.

Third, look at the behavior, not only the number. Read transcripts. Look at the failure modes. Sometimes a model gets the right answer for the wrong reasons, or games the grader, and you only catch that by looking closely. Qualitative review sounds unglamorous, but it's one of the highest-leverage things a research team can do.

And finally, the evals that matter most are increasingly the ones that look like real work: long-horizon tasks, agentic settings, messy real-world problems where there isn't a clean multiple-choice answer. They're harder to build and harder to grade, but that's where the frontier is now. If you build your eval culture around those, you naturally avoid a lot of the benchmark-maxing trap, because there's no easy shortcut to doing real tasks well.

r001.rationale: Recommends combining public benchmarks, held-out and internal evals, qualitative review, and evaluations of real-world tasks.

r002.rationale: Recommends investing in internal, held-out evaluations that refresh over time and use fresh problems.

r003.rationale: Says public benchmarks remain useful as sanity checks; they lose value when people optimize for them, not simply when they become public.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot. The honest answer is that benchmark maxing is kind of a natural consequence of how incentives work in the field. If a number goes up and everyone pays attention to that number, people will optimize for it, whether or not it reflects real capability.

The way I'd frame it is that evals should be a diagnostic tool, not the objective. The moment an eval becomes the thing you're training toward, it stops telling you anything useful. So internally, we try to hold ourselves to a few things.

First, you want a healthy separation between what you look at during development and what you treat as a real held-out signal. If your researchers are iterating against a benchmark every day, that benchmark is contaminated in spirit, even if the literal test set never touched the training data. You need some set of evals you deliberately don't look at very often, so that when you do, it means something.

Second, the evals that matter most are the ones that are closest to what people actually do with the model. Static multiple-choice datasets saturate fast, and a model can learn the shape of the questions without learning the underlying skill. We've found it much more informative to look at things like long-horizon agentic tasks, real codebases, or problems where the model has to produce something a human expert would actually use. Those are harder to game because there isn't a trick to the format.

Third, you should be suspicious of your own wins. When a number jumps, the first question should be "why," not "great." Is it generalizing, or did we leak something, or did we overfit to the style of the grader? We've had cases where a result looked fantastic and on closer inspection the model had learned a shortcut. Catching that early is part of doing evals well.

And then I think there's a cultural piece. If the only thing that gets celebrated is the leaderboard, people will chase the leaderboard. You have to reward the researchers who find out a model is worse than it looks, because that's the information that actually helps you build a better model. Benchmarks are a proxy. The goal is capability that holds up when real people use the thing, and if you keep that front of mind, you naturally end up treating evals with more humility.

r001.rationale: Recommends using several kinds of evaluations, including held-out signals and realistic tasks such as agentic work and real codebases, to assess capability.

r002.rationale: Does not recommend continually creating new evaluations.

r003.rationale: Says an evaluation loses usefulness when researchers optimize against it; does not say public availability itself makes it cease to be a good evaluation.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with what you actually want the model to do, rather than which benchmark you want to win. A benchmark is a proxy, and if you spend enough time optimizing against it, you can improve the score without improving the underlying capability very much.

So I’d want a mix of evaluations: held-out tests, tasks that reflect real usage, and human feedback. And then I’d look closely at where those disagree. If your benchmark goes up but people aren’t finding the model more useful, that’s a signal to investigate, not just celebrate the number.

You also have to keep refreshing the evaluations. Look at failures, build tests around the capabilities those failures expose, and keep a separate set that you’re not using to guide every development decision. The goal is for the evaluation to tell you something you didn’t already know.

r001.rationale: It recommends a mix of held-out tests, real-usage tasks, and human feedback to assess the model.

r002.rationale: It recommends continually refreshing evaluations and building new tests around observed failures.

r003.rationale: It recommends keeping a separate evaluation set, but does not say that evaluations stop being good once publicly available.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with what you actually want the model to do for people, and then work backward to the evaluation. If you start with a benchmark and optimize against it long enough, you can get a higher score without making the model more useful.

So I’d want a mix: held-out evaluations that you don’t constantly tune against, realistic tasks that test the whole workflow, and feedback from people using the model. And you have to look at the failures, not just the aggregate number. Did it misunderstand the task? Did it make something up? Did it get stuck and fail to recover?

The benchmark should be evidence that you’re making progress. It shouldn’t become the definition of progress.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a mix of held-out evaluations, realistic workflow tasks, and feedback from model users.

r002.rationale: It does not recommend continually creating new evaluations.

r003.rationale: It warns that optimizing against a benchmark can inflate scores without improving usefulness, but does not say an evaluation stops being good once it becomes public.
